appearance.size: 65 to 95 mm head-body; tail 60 to 105 mm
appearance.summary: Small slender rodent, fur light brown to black with a white or buffy belly, long sparsely furred tail with circular rows of scales.

records.behavior: Generally nocturnal, though some are active by day in human dwellings. Dwells in cracks in rocks or walls, or in underground burrows with tunnels, nesting and storage chambers, and three or four exits; with humans, nests behind rafters, in woodpiles, or storage areas. Quick runner (up to 8 miles per hour), good climber and jumper, swims well, yet rarely travels more than 50 feet from its home. Territorial and colonial when commensal; dominant males hold a territory with several females and their young. Communicates by squeaks, pheromones, and (in males exposed to female pheromones) complex ultrasonic songs; whiskers feel air movements and surface textures.
records.conservation_note: Animal Diversity Web: commensal populations generally stable, densities as high as 10 mice per square meter; wild populations less stable; overall populations flourishing and aided by human construction. As an introduced species, no GB Red List assessment has been made (PTES).
records.conservation_status: Least Concern (global, per People's Trust for Endangered Species)

records.diet: Omnivore. In the wild: seeds, fleshy roots, leaves and stems, plus insects (beetle larvae, caterpillars, cockroaches) and carrion when available. In human habitation: any accessible human food, plus glue, soap, and other household materials. Many store food.
records.habitat: Houses, barns, granaries, cultivated fields, fencerows, and wooded areas; seldom strays far from buildings. Some individuals spend summer in fields and move into barns and houses with cool autumn weather.

records.reproduction: Polygynous; breeding year-round, though wild mice may breed only April to September. Estrous cycle 4-6 days; gestation 19-21 days (longer if lactating); 5-10 litters per year when conditions suit, up to 14 reported; litters of 3-12, generally 5 or 6, born naked and blind, furred by 10 days, eyes open at 14 days, weaned at 3 weeks, sexually mature at 5-7 weeks. Wild lifespan mostly 12-18 months; about 2 years in captivity, up to 6 years reported for individuals.

subspecies.note: No verified subspecies list this pass. Animal Diversity Web notes the name often refers to several fairly distinct kinds of mice, and that as many as seven separate species may be placed under Mus musculus, such as Mus domesticus (western European house mice) and Mus castaneus (southeastern Asian house mice).

appearance.size: Head-body 455 to 900 mm; tail 300 to 555 mm
appearance.summary: Largest of the Vulpes species. Upper parts pale yellowish red to deep reddish brown, underside white, ashy, or slaty; lower legs usually black; tail usually white- or black-tipped. Cross foxes (reddish brown with a black back stripe and shoulder stripe) are about 25% of individuals; silver foxes (strong silver to nearly black) about 10%. Eyes yellow in mature animals; nose dark brown or black.
appearance.weight: 3 to 14 kg; males slightly larger than females; northern populations larger (Bergmann's rule)

records.behavior: Solitary; does not form packs like wolves. At least partly territorial; ranges occupied by an adult male and one or two adult females with young. Home range 5-12 square km in good habitat, 20-50 square km in poorer habitat. Main earthen dens plus emergency burrows; often takes over dens of rabbits or marmots; same den often used over generations. Nocturnal or crepuscular; top speed about 48 km/h; can leap obstacles 2 m high. Pups disperse 10 km to almost 400 km in the autumn after birth. 28 kinds of vocalizations described; individuals have distinguishable voices. Characteristic mouse hunting: stands motionless listening and watching, then leaps high and brings forelimbs straight down to pin the mouse.
records.conservation_note: Animal Diversity Web: overall populations stable and expanding their range in response to human changes in habitats. Three subspecies listed in CITES Appendix III.
records.conservation_status: Least Concern (IUCN, per Animal Diversity Web / Encyclopedia of Life summary)

records.reproduction: Mating varies: often monogamous, sometimes polygynous, sometimes with non-breeding female helpers. Estrous 1-6 days; breeding December-January in the south, January-February central, February-April in the north. Gestation typically 51-53 days (range 49-56). Litters 1-13 pups, average 5; birth weight 50-150 g; born blind, eyes open 9-14 days; leave den at 4-5 weeks; weaned by 8-10 weeks; remain with parents until autumn; sexually mature by 10 months. Lifespan 10-12 years in captivity, average 3 years in the wild.

subspecies.note: No verified subspecies list this pass. Animal Diversity Web notes three subspecies are listed in CITES Appendix III (names not verified this pass).

records.tracks_sign: Oval prints showing four toes with claws and a separate heel pad; front tracks oval, hind tracks diamond-shaped. Mississippi State Extension figures: 1.75-2.5 inches long by 1.5-2 inches wide; walking pattern often straight, prints 8-15 inches apart, tracks often show hair marks. A fox sets its hind foot exactly in the spot left by its forefoot. Scent marking is extensive: urine, feces, anal sac secretions, the supracaudal gland, and glands around lips, jaw, and foot pads.

appearance.summary: Medium-sized songbird with a thick bright orange cone-shaped beak, long tail, and a pointed crest. Male bright red all over except a large black face mask covering eyes, beak area, and throat. Female light brown with a reddish crest, wings, and tail.

records.behavior: Monogamous, though often a different mate each breeding season. Pairs form in early spring; the male courts with crest raised, swaying side to side while singing softly. Usually raises two broods a year, one beginning around March and the second late May to July; breeding season March to September. Female builds the nest and incubates; chicks hatch featherless and are brooded by the female for at least 2 days. Known to attack its own reflection; aggressive and territorial.
records.conservation_note: IUCN category not verified from a primary source this pass. DLIA species page: quite common, not listed as being of any special conservation concern, range extending in the north. Secondary summaries report Least Concern and a population around 100 million, but those figures were not adopted without a primary source.

appearance.size: Sea-run fish 2.3 to 9.1 kg; commercially caught average 4.5 to 5.4 kg
appearance.summary: Graceful fish, deepening rearward from a small pointed head to the deepest point under the dorsal fin, then tapering to a slender caudal peduncle with a spreading, slightly emarginate caudal fin. Fewer than 13 anal fin rays (distinguishes it from Pacific salmon). Parr have 8-11 pigmented bars per side alternating with a single row of red spots along the lateral line; at sea, silvery sides and belly, back brown/green/blue, with numerous X-shaped black spots; spawning fish turn bronze-purple with reddish spots; spent kelts are so dark they are called black salmon.
appearance.weight: World record rod-caught: 35.89 kg, Tana River, Norway

records.behavior: Migratory and nomadic. Young swim in schools; many rivers' fish share ocean areas. Returns to its natal river to spawn, guided largely by the odor of the parent stream imprinted during the smolt migration; sun, stars, and the taste of home water are also suggested. Ceases feeding before spawning and does not eat after re-entering fresh water. Unlike Pacific salmon, Atlantic salmon can survive spawning and return to sea to spawn again.
records.conservation_note: Current IUCN assessment not verified this pass. The 1999 ADW account reports the species as listed lower risk by IUCN and considered an endangered species by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, and describes North America's large-salmon population as at its lowest point in history, with habitat destruction, dams, overfishing, pollution, and acid rain taking their toll. Treat the 1999 wording as dated, not current.

records.diet: Carnivore. Stream young eat mainly aquatic insect larvae (blackflies, stoneflies, caddisflies, chironomids) plus terrestrial insects, especially in late summer. At sea: euphausiids, amphipods, decapods, and fishes such as herring, alewives, smelts, capelin, small mackerel, sand lance, and small cod.
records.habitat: Anadromous. Fresh water for at least the first 2-3 years of life; relatively large cool rivers with extensive gravelly bottom headwaters are essential early. Smolts migrate to sea for 1-2 years; at sea prefers 4-12 C water.

records.reproduction: Spawns October-November, peak usually late October. Males develop an elongated head with a pronounced hook (kype) on the lower jaw. Female chooses a gravel-bottom riffle above a pool and digs the redd by flapping with her caudal fin; eggs and sperm are released together; average 700-800 eggs per pound of female body weight; eggs pale orange, large, spherical. Female covers eggs with gravel, then repeats with new redds until spawning is done (a week or more). Eggs hatch usually in April; young remain in gravel until the yolk sac is absorbed, emerging May-June the following year. Life stages: alevin, parr (to about 65 mm), smolt (12-15 cm, ready for sea), grilse (return after 1 year at sea) or 2 sea-year salmon. Some die after spawning; many survive to spawn a second time; very few spawn three or more times. No parental investment beyond spawning.

subspecies.note: No verified subspecies list this pass. Landlocked salmon is a life-history form (fish living entirely in fresh water), listed as an alternate name, not a subspecies claim.

records.tracks_sign: No footprints for a fish. The equivalent sign is the redd: a gravel nest dug by the female in a riffle above a pool, plus the seasonal upstream run itself. Eggs are buried in gravel at 12.7 to 25.4 cm depth.

appearance.summary: Large orange and black butterfly. Upper wings tawny-orange with black veins and margins and two series of small white spots in the margins; undersides similar with yellow-brown wingtips and larger white spots. Males have a small black spot on the hindwing and thinner wing veins; females have darker veins. Caterpillars about 2 inches at maturity, ringed black, white, and yellow, with two long thin filaments on the thorax and one on the abdomen.

records.behavior: The only butterfly species making a two-way migration. Massive fall migrations August-October, flying thousands of miles south to hibernate along the California coast and in central Mexico; a few overwinter along the Gulf or south Atlantic coast. Travels as much as 100 miles a day on migration; stops to feed on nectar and roost together at night. Adults warm up by basking with wings open toward the sun. Poisonous to vertebrate predators: caterpillars store cardiac glycosides from milkweed, and adults retain them; birds that eat one vomit and learn to avoid the pattern.
records.conservation_note: Current IUCN assessment not verified this pass. An older secondary summary lists Near Threatened (IUCN 3.1); that figure was not adopted as current. Butterflies and Moths of North America lists NCGR G5 (demonstrably secure globally, though rare at range periphery). Milkweed loss is cited by read sources as a driver of decline.

records.diet: Caterpillars eat milkweed only: common milkweed (Asclepias syriaca), swamp milkweed (A. incarnata), showy milkweed (A. speciosa), and milkweed vines in the tropics; also other genera including Calotropis, Cynanchum, Gonolobus, and Sarcostemma. Adults feed on nectar from many flowers, especially milkweed nectar, plus dogbane, lilac, red clover, lantana, thistles, goldenrods, blazing stars, ironweed, and tickseed sunflowers; also fruit juice.
records.habitat: Open sunny areas with host plants: fields, meadows, weedy areas, marshes, roadsides, gardens, prairies, and grasslands. Prefers warmer climates; cannot tolerate frost. Requires thick tree cover at winter roosts (oyamel fir in Mexico; eucalyptus and Monterey pine groves in California).
